# Use the specified ARM64 base image with Flux, OpenMPI, and AWS EFA support
FROM ghcr.io/converged-computing/flux-openmpi:ubuntu2204-efa-arm

# Set environment variables to avoid interactive prompts during package installation
ENV DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive

# Set the version of OSU benchmarks to build
ENV OSU_VERSION=7.3

# One RUN command to install dependencies, download, build, install the application, and clean up
RUN apt-get update && \
    # Install build dependencies and necessary utilities including ca-certificates
    apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    build-essential \
    ca-certificates \
    wget \
    && \
    # Create a temporary directory for the build
    mkdir -p /tmp/build && cd /tmp/build && \
    # Download the OSU benchmarks source code
    wget "https://mvapich.cse.ohio-state.edu/download/mvapich/osu-micro-benchmarks-${OSU_VERSION}.tar.gz" && \
    # Extract the source code
    tar -xvf "osu-micro-benchmarks-${OSU_VERSION}.tar.gz" && \
    cd "osu-micro-benchmarks-${OSU_VERSION}" && \
    # Set the C and CXX compilers to the MPI wrappers as required
    export CC=mpicc CXX=mpicxx && \
    # Configure the build. The MPI compilers will automatically enable MPI support.
    # We install to a temporary prefix before copying the executables to the final location.
    ./configure --prefix=/usr/local/osu && \
    # Compile the benchmarks
    make -j$(nproc) && \
    # Install the compiled benchmarks to the specified prefix
    make install && \
    # Copy the compiled benchmark executables to a directory on the system's PATH
    # This is a robust way to find all executables within the MPI benchmark suite
    find /usr/local/osu/libexec/osu-micro-benchmarks/mpi -type f -executable -exec cp {} /usr/local/bin/ \; && \
    # Clean up the build directory and source files
    cd / && rm -rf /tmp/build && \
    # Clean up the temporary installation prefix
    rm -rf /usr/local/osu && \
    # Clean up the apt package cache to reduce image size
    apt-get clean && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

# Set a default command to show the path to a key benchmark, confirming it's available
CMD ["which", "osu_latency"]

flux-minicluster-manifest.item:
# This MiniCluster manifest is designed to run the OSU Latency benchmark
# across two nodes on an AWS ARM-based Kubernetes cluster.
# It leverages the Flux Operator for scheduling and MPI bootstrapping.
apiVersion: flux-framework.org/v1alpha2
kind: MiniCluster
metadata:
  # Name for the MiniCluster job, indicating its purpose and environment.
  name: osu-latency-aws-arm-cpu
  # Deploy to the 'default' namespace as requested.
  namespace: default
spec:
  # The number of pods in the MiniCluster. For this test, we want one pod per node.
  size: 2
  # The total number of MPI ranks to run. osu_latency runs between two processes.
  tasks: 2

  # Set to true to enable strict validation of the MiniCluster spec.
  logging:
    strict: true

  # Do not automatically delete the job and pods upon completion for debugging/inspection.
  cleanup: false

  # Flux-specific configuration.
  flux:
    # Specify the architecture for ARM-based AWS instances.
    arch: "arm"
    container:
      # Although the flux sidecar container is disabled, the ARM-compatible image is specified
      # as requested, in case the operator logic requires it.
      image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/flux-view-ubuntu:arm-jammy
      # Disable the flux sidecar container. This requires Flux to be pre-installed
      # in the main application container.
      disable: true

  # Define the main application container.
  containers:
    - image: ghcr.io/converged-computing/fractale-agent-experiments:osu-latency
      # Ensure the latest version of the container image is always pulled.
      imagePullPolicy: Always
      # This is a worker container, not a launcher container. This MUST be false.
      launcher: false
      # Command to run the OSU Latency benchmark.
      # The Flux Operator will automatically wrap this with 'flux run -n 2 -N 2 ...'
      command: osu_latency
      # Request AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) for high-performance networking.
      # This is crucial for HPC workloads on AWS to get low-latency, high-bandwidth interconnect.
      resources:
        limits:
          vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1"
        requests:
          vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: "1"

manager.name: Build and Deploy OSU Latency
manager.description: Build a Docker container and deploy it as a Kubernetes Job.

context.environment: AWS CPU instance in Kubernetes to run across nodes
context.details:
You MUST use ghcr.io/converged-computing/flux-openmpi:ubuntu2204-efa-arm as a base image. It includes OpenMPI and libfabric provided from the efa installer for AWS and the entire Flux Framework stack.
You MUST compile setting the cxx compiler to mpicxx and the c compiler to mpicc.
Build the OSU benchmarks. You MUST have MPI support enabled. You MUST ensure osu_latency is on the path.
You MUST build for a multi-node MPI environment

context.resources: The resource spec you got earlier is for an autoscaling cluster, so the nodes possible are not there. You must add the nodeSelector to use node.kubernetes.io/instance-type m7g.16xlarge with 64 CPU, 256 GiB Memory, ARM (Graviton3).
context.details:
Run The OSU Latency benchmark across 2 nodes.
You MUST run on 2 nodes and you MUST set flux.container.disable to true.
You MUST set the containers imagePullPolicy to Always.
The Flux Operator uses flux run in the pwd with the tasks determined by the spec.tasks.
You MUST set resource requests and limits to use vpc.amazonaws.com/efa: 1
Since this is an ARM instance you MUST change the flux.container.image to be
ghcr.io/converged-computing/flux-view-ubuntu:arm-jammy and set flux.arch: "arm".
